ai.definition: Molecular assemblers are theoretical devices capable of arranging individual atoms and molecules with atomic precision to form any desired molecular structure or material.
ai.howItWorks: These devices operate by using a large number (billions) of parallel scanning tunneling microscopy heads, each capable of manipulating single atoms or molecules. The heads work in concert to build complex structures atom by atom.
ai.problemSolved: Current limitations in manufacturing precision and the ability to create arbitrary materials at the molecular level prevent widespread production of advanced materials with desired properties.
ai.manufacturing: The technology is currently theoretical, so no specific manufacturing process exists. However, it would involve highly specialized equipment and processes for atom manipulation on a large scale.
ai.buildProcess: Building molecular assemblers involves developing ultra-precise nanoscale tools capable of manipulating individual atoms or molecules in parallel. This requires significant advances in materials science, electronics, and microfabrication techniques.
ai.costDrivers: High development costs due to the need for cutting-edge research, specialized equipment, and large-scale production challenges. Energy-intensive fabrication processes would also drive up costs.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is in the early stages of theoretical exploration and has not yet reached a point where practical applications can be developed or commercialized.
ai.regulation: Currently, no specific regulations apply as the technology does not exist. However, once it becomes feasible, regulatory frameworks will need to address safety, environmental impact, and ethical considerations.
ai.risks: Technological feasibility is uncertain; potential misuse in creating harmful substances; high financial risk due to unproven commercial viability; environmental risks from byproducts of manufacturing processes.
ai.profitability: Uncertain at this stage. If successful, the technology could revolutionize materials science and manufacturing but requires significant investment and time before any return on investment can be realized.
ai.futureDevelopment: Further research is needed to develop practical implementations, including advancements in nanotechnology, electronics, and materials science. Collaboration between academia, industry, and government will likely be crucial.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units would draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication processes are energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and precise control requirements.

glossary.def: A technique for imaging surfaces at the atomic scale by using a sharp probe that is brought very close to the surface of a sample.
A field of study dealing with the design, characterization, and application of structures, devices, and systems by controlling matter on an atomic or molecular scale (typically 1-100 nanometers).

subsystems.name: Positioning and manipulation
subsystems.role: moves reactive molecules with atomic precision.

subsystems.name: Reactive tooling
subsystems.role: forms and breaks specific chemical bonds on demand.

subsystems.name: Feedstock and waste handling
subsystems.role: delivers molecular building blocks and removes byproducts.

subsystems.name: Control and sensing
subsystems.role: senses the atomic environment and guides each placement.

subsystems.name: Structural framework
subsystems.role: holds manipulators in precise relative positions.

subsystems.name: Power and communication
subsystems.role: supplies energy and coordination signals to each unit.

buildSteps.title: Design the target and reaction pathway
buildSteps.detail: Use computational chemistry to plan which bonds to form in what order and which molecular tools can catalyse each step.

buildSteps.title: Synthesize the molecular tools
buildSteps.detail: Make reactive tip molecules and building blocks using existing synthetic chemistry and, where possible, self-assembly such as DNA origami or designed proteins.

buildSteps.title: Build a single mechanosynthetic unit
buildSteps.detail: Attach a reactive tip to a scanning probe or molecular arm, then use it to form a simple bond under controlled conditions in vacuum or liquid.

buildSteps.title: Demonstrate atomic precision
buildSteps.detail: Show that the unit can place a specific atom or group at a chosen site, with repeated success and minimal error.

buildSteps.title: Parallelize the manipulators
buildSteps.detail: Fabricate arrays of thousands to billions of identical units on a chip, each independently addressable, to overcome the slow speed of a single tip.

buildSteps.title: Integrate feedstock and control
buildSteps.detail: Add nanoscale channels for delivering reactants, removing waste, and wiring for feedback control.

buildSteps.title: Bootstrap to higher complexity
buildSteps.detail: Use early assemblers to build more capable assemblers, gradually increasing the range of materials they can make.

buildSteps.title: Demonstrate universal fabrication
buildSteps.detail: Produce a macroscopic object, such as a diamond-like material, from simple feedstock to prove general-purpose manufacturing.

buildSteps.title: Scale to manufacturing
buildSteps.detail: Design factories where many assemblers work in parallel to produce practical quantities of useful materials.

prerequisites.why: scanning probe microscopes can move individual atoms and molecules, but only slowly and one at a time.
forces from probe tips have driven specific chemical reactions, but not yet in a general, programmable way.
DNA origami and protein design create precise nanoscale scaffolds, but cannot yet build arbitrary covalent structures.
there is no established way to deliver energy and control signals to billions of independent nanoscale machines.
a practical assembler must detect and fix mistakes in bonds and positions, which no system does today.
controlling billions of manipulators simultaneously with atomic precision is an unsolved engineering problem.

pathway.milestone: single-atom manipulation and self-assembled nanostructures in the lab
pathway.unlocks: basic tools and understanding of atomic-scale fabrication.

pathway.milestone: mechanosynthetic reactions that build small molecules with atomic precision
pathway.unlocks: proof that molecular tools can make specific covalent bonds.

pathway.milestone: parallel arrays of thousands of independently controlled probes
pathway.unlocks: practical throughput for making useful quantities of a material.

pathway.milestone: a self-replicating molecular assembler that can copy itself
pathway.unlocks: exponential scaling of production without building each unit by hand.

pathway.milestone: universal fabrication of complex macroscopic products from simple feedstock
